title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and two bounds lower and upper, count how many contiguous subarrays have a sum that falls within the inclusive range from lower to upper. Solve it with prefix sums and a merge-sort-based counting technique and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

s1_definition.profdef: The count of range sum problem asks how many contiguous subarrays have a sum lying within an inclusive range from lower to upper. It is solved with prefix sums reframed as pairs: a subarray sum lies in the range exactly when, for a given right prefix, the matching left prefix lies in a shifted window, and counting such pairs efficiently across all prefixes is done with a modified merge sort that counts qualifying pairs while sorting, achieving n log n time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows that can be positive or negative and wants to count how many continuous stretches had a net total between a lower and an upper regulatory threshold, because stretches in that band require a specific disclosure. He turns each stretch total into a comparison between two running totals, then uses an efficient divide-and-conquer count so he does not have to compare every pair of days by hand.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count prefix-sum pairs whose difference lies in the range, efficiently, with a merge-sort that counts during the merge.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The count of range sum problem asks how many contiguous subarrays have a sum lying within an inclusive range from lower to upper. It is solved with prefix sums reframed as pairs: a subarray sum lies in the range exactly when, for a given right prefix, the matching left prefix lies in a shifted window, and counting such pairs efficiently across all prefixes is done with a modified merge sort that counts qualifying pairs while sorting, achieving n log n time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows that can be positive or negative and wants to count how many continuous stretches had a net total between a lower and an upper regulatory threshold, because stretches in that band require a specific disclosure. He turns each stretch total into a comparison between two running totals, then uses an efficient divide-and-conquer count so he does not have to compare every pair of days by hand.

**One line to remember:** Count prefix-sum pairs whose difference lies in the range, efficiently, with a merge-sort that counts during the merge.

sections.s2_technical:
We start from prefix sums. Let P at zero be zero and P at i be the sum of the first i elements. The sum of the subarray covering indices j to i minus one is P at i minus P at j. We want to count pairs j less than i such that P at i minus P at j lies between lower and upper inclusive. Rearranged, for each right index i we need the count of left indices j less than i with P at j in the interval from P at i minus upper to P at i minus lower.

Counting those pairs naively for every i is quadratic. The classic efficient method embeds the counting inside a merge sort over the prefix-sum array. During the merge step, when the left half and the right half are each sorted, we can, for each prefix value in the right half, slide two pointers over the left half to count how many left values fall into the required shifted interval, and because both halves are sorted these pointer scans are linear per merge level. Summing across the log n levels of merging gives n log n total pair-counting work.

Concretely we recursively sort the prefix array; at each merge we first count: for each index in the right portion we advance a low pointer while the left value is too small, meaning P at i minus P at left is still above upper, and advance a high pointer while the left value keeps the difference at or above lower, and the gap between the pointers is the count of qualifying left endpoints for that right endpoint. Then we perform the normal merge to keep the array sorted for the parent call. The senior-level nuance is that the counting must use the original prefix order semantics, which is preserved because we only ever count pairs where the right index came from a later position than the left, a property the divide-and-conquer structure maintains.

We use long prefix sums to avoid overflow, especially since subtracting bounds can push values far. The time complexity is O(n log n) and the space complexity is O(n) for the prefix array and merge buffers. An alternative is a balanced BST or a Fenwick tree over coordinate-compressed prefix values, also n log n, which some interviewers prefer; the merge-sort method is the most self-contained. This problem is a genuine hard-tier application of prefix sums combined with order-statistics counting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the regulatory-reporting team reviews a sequence of daily net flows that can be positive or negative and must count how many continuous stretches had a net total falling within a specific regulatory band, from a lower threshold to an upper threshold, because any stretch whose net lands in that band triggers a mandatory disclosure. They need an exact count across all possible stretches. This is exactly the count-of-range-sum problem.

Problem 2 — Comparing every possible stretch is quadratic and does not scale to long histories across many accounts. The prefix-sum plus merge-sort counting method computes the exact count in n log n time, which keeps the regulatory-count job within its reporting window.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `RangeSumCounter` service with a `countStretchesInBand` method implementing the merge-sort counting over prefix sums, and a runnable `CountOfRangeSumDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's flow sequences against a lower and upper band, logging each merge-level count at fine level and the final total at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's flows are -2, 5, -1 with band lower minus 2 and upper 2. First we build the prefix array of length four: prefix at 0 is 0, prefix at 1 is minus 2, prefix at 2 is 3, prefix at 3 is 2.

The counting works on pairs of prefix indices where the right index is greater than the left and the difference of their prefixes lies in the band. Enumerating the valid stretches directly for clarity: the stretch from index 0 to 0 is just minus 2, which is in the band. The stretch from index 1 to 1 is 5, not in the band. The stretch from index 2 to 2 is minus 1, in the band. The stretch from index 0 to 1 is minus 2 plus 5 equals 3, not in the band. The stretch from index 1 to 2 is 5 minus 1 equals 4, not in the band. The stretch from index 0 to 2 is minus 2 plus 5 minus 1 equals 2, in the band.

So three stretches qualify: the single day minus 2, the single day minus 1, and the whole stretch summing to 2. The merge-sort counting arrives at this same total of 3 by counting, during each merge, how many sorted left prefixes fall into each right prefix's shifted interval, which is the efficient equivalent of the direct enumeration above.

The count of in-band stretches for Rajesh is 3.

```
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) flows
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Merge [0,4) running count = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Stretches with net in [-2, 2] over [-2, 5, -1] = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar stretches in band = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Stretches with net in [-2, 2] over [0, 0] = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma stretches in band = 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: flows [-2,5,-1], band [-2, 2]
    │
    ▼
  RangeSumCounter.countStretchesInBand()
    │ prefix = [0, -2, 3, 2]
    │
    ▼
  mergeCount(prefix, 0, 4)   (divide & conquer)
    │ split → [0,2) and [2,4), recurse, then COUNT across halves:
    │   for each right prefix r: #left in [P[r]-upper, P[r]-lower]
    │   (two sorted pointers low/high advance linearly per merge)
    │ then merge to keep sorted for parent
    │
    ├─ equivalent direct enumeration:
    │   [0..0]=-2  [2..2]=-1  [0..2]=2   (others out of band)
    │
    ▼
  Output: 3   (n log n counting)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The count of range sum problem asks how many contiguous subarrays have a sum within an inclusive range from lower to upper, and I solve it in n log n time with prefix sums plus a merge-sort-based counting technique. I build prefix sums so that any subarray sum is the difference of two prefixes, and then a subarray sum lies in the range exactly when, for a given right prefix, the matching left prefix falls in the shifted interval from the right prefix minus upper to the right prefix minus lower. Counting such pairs naively is quadratic, so I embed the counting inside a merge sort.

During each merge, with the left and right halves already sorted, I slide two pointers over the left half for each prefix in the right half: one pointer advances past left values that are too small and the other past left values that keep the difference at or above lower, and the gap between the pointers is the count of qualifying left endpoints. These pointer scans are linear per merge level, and summed over the log n levels they give n log n total counting work, after which I perform the ordinary merge so the array stays sorted for the parent call.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the regulatory-reporting team. Daily net flows could be positive or negative, and we had to count how many continuous stretches had a net total falling within a specific regulatory band, because any stretch landing in that band triggered a mandatory disclosure. We needed an exact count across all possible stretches, and the prefix-sum plus merge-sort counting computed it in n log n time, which kept the nightly regulatory-count job within its reporting window across long histories.

The senior-level point I make is that this is a genuine hard-tier problem because it fuses prefix sums with order-statistics counting, and recognizing that the counting can ride along inside a merge sort, or equivalently inside a Fenwick tree over coordinate-compressed prefix values, is the key insight. I mention both implementations because interviewers differ on which they prefer, and I always stress using long prefix sums since subtracting the bounds can push values far and overflow is a real risk on monetary data. Offering the merge-sort and Fenwick alternatives and flagging the overflow safeguard is what signals to an interviewer that I have the depth to handle the hardest prefix-sum questions.
